intro:
Join the PyCon HK 2026 Development Sprint on Sunday, 15 November: a day of community collaboration on Python and open-source projects. Come ready to contribute, share ideas and learn together; this is not a taught workshop.

We are finalizing the projects and detailed arrangements. Read the Sprint Q&A to learn what to expect and how to prepare. Admission is free; register for Sprint Day separately from Conference Day.

On-site registration: 15 November 2026 at 10:00 Hong Kong time (UTC+8).

qa.question: What is a Development Sprint?
qa.answer:
A Development Sprint is a collaborative working session for open-source projects. Participants work with project maintainers and other contributors on useful tasks, share knowledge and learn by doing. Contributions can include code, tests, documentation, translation and other work that a project needs.

This is a community collaboration day, not a taught workshop or a step-by-step lesson. Come ready to contribute in a way that fits your experience.

qa.question: What will I do on Sprint Day?
qa.answer: Choose a project you are interested in, discuss a suitable task with its lead or contributors, and work on it together. Read the project's contribution and setup instructions when they are available. The detailed 2026 timetable and project arrangements will be announced when confirmed.

qa.question: How is Sprint Day different from Conference Day?
qa.answer: Conference Day on 14 November centres on talks, sessions and community activities. Sprint Day on 15 November focuses on working together on Python and open-source projects. They are separate activities and require separate ticket registration.

qa.question: Who is Sprint Day for?
qa.answer: Anyone interested in Python, open source or collaborative learning is welcome, including experienced contributors and people making their first contribution. You do not need to bring your own project. Look for a project whose goals and tasks match your interests.

qa.question: Can Python beginners take part?
qa.answer: Yes. The event welcomes newcomers as well as experienced contributors. Tell the project lead what you have tried and what you would like to learn. Depending on the project, a first task could involve documentation, translation, reproducing a problem or a small code change; available tasks and support vary by project.

qa.question: What should I bring and prepare?
qa.answer: Bring a laptop capable of running the tools for your chosen project, its charger and any adapters you need. Before the event, read the project's README, contribution guide and setup instructions when available, and prepare the accounts it uses, such as GitHub. Check the individual project's requirements before attending.

qa.question: Can I come to observe and learn before contributing?
qa.answer: If you want to observe, register for Sprint Day and speak with the project lead or organizing team about how to join the group. You can explain your interests and experience, learn how the project works and agree on a suitable way to participate. Please respect the group's working space and discussions.

qa.question: What if I need to arrive late or leave early?
qa.answer: Coordinate with the project lead or organizing team in advance. Let the group know when you expect to arrive or leave, so you can agree on a task and hand over any work. Check the confirmed timetable and entry instructions before travelling.

qa.question: Is Sprint Day free, and do I need a separate ticket?
qa.answer: Admission to PyCon HK 2026 is free, but Sprint Day on 15 November and Conference Day on 14 November require separate tickets. Use the registration button to register for the day or days you plan to attend. Optional contributions, T-shirts and PyNight are separate from free Sprint Day admission.

qa.question: Can I propose my own project?
qa.answer:
Yes. The published 2026 announcement invites proposals for Python and open-source Sprint projects. Use the call for Sprint projects and leads to describe your project, what you would like to work on and how others can contribute. Submitting a proposal does not by itself confirm a place in the programme.

The Sprint submission deadline is 14 November 2026 at 23:59 Hong Kong time (UTC+8).

qa.question: How do I become a Sprint Lead?
qa.answer: Use the call for Sprint projects and leads to submit your interest. A lead helps introduce the project, explain its setup and contribution process, and identify tasks that participants can work on together. Include the preparation participants will need and the kinds of contributions you can support.

qa.question: Which projects and Sprint Leads are taking part?
qa.answer: Luciano Scarpulla leads nsh-py, which brings native desktop UIs to plain Python. Sam Lau leads Training an LLM with MiniMind. Soojin Yoon (Luna) leads a Django sprint with two tracks: code and tests, and documentation translation. See the project goals and preparation steps on the Sprint Day page.

location: Hong Kong Institute of Information Technology (HKIIT), IVE (Lee Wai Lee), Tseung Kwan O

contributions: Develop styled badges, alerts, inputs, lists and layouts, with headless tests.
Work toward macOS and Windows parity with Linux, including Ctrl-C handling.
Improve signal API ergonomics and build counter, form and pandas-table examples.
Write and improve documentation, setup guides and examples.
Explore prebuilt Python wheels to reduce the need for a Rust toolchain.
projects.title: nsh-py: native desktop UIs in plain Python
projects.description:
Join Luciano to work on Python bindings for Native Shell (NSH), with Sprint goals covering styled components, examples and macOS/Windows/Linux support. The repository link is the upstream NSH project. Python-specific setup instructions will be added when available. The aim is for each participant to contribute a merged PR.

All levels are welcome, including examples and documentation; Rust is optional. Bring a macOS, Windows or Linux laptop.

contributions: Try chatting with the trained model.
projects.title: Training an LLM with MiniMind
projects.description: Use MiniMind, a lightweight framework with a model architecture aligned with Qwen3, to learn how to train a small language model at low cost.

contributions: Make progress on one concrete contribution, such as reproducing a bug or writing a regression test.
Learn how to continue contributing after the sprint.
projects.title: Django Code and Test Sprint
projects.description: Work in small groups on a code or test task from the Django issue tracker. First-time contributors are welcome.

contributions: Make progress on a concrete contribution, such as reviewing a translation.
Learn how to continue contributing after the sprint.
projects.title: Django Documentation Translation Sprint
projects.description:
Work in small groups to improve Django’s documentation translations on Transifex. First-time contributors are welcome.

Before the sprint, open the django-docs project and click Join this project. Sign in or create a Transifex account, select your language and request to join its team. Apply early so your team has time to review your request. You can start translating once approved. New translators can also introduce themselves on the Django Internationalization Forum.
